problem: Existing pedestrian simulators for social robot navigation need manually specified agents, goals and behaviors per scenario, apply uniform behavior models, and rely on SFM as the sole navigation primitive, so simulated pedestrians behave implausibly in structured environments.
motivation: Social robot navigation needs diverse, realistic and easily generated human crowd scenarios to close the sim2real gap. Prior text-driven crowd generators (Text-Crowd, TRACE) lack semantic grounding or simulator integration, and HuNavSim's behavior trees send goals directly to SFM without waypoints, producing straight-line paths through walls.
key_idea: Generate pedestrian simulations from free text by having an LLM with RAG produce behavior trees grounded in a semantic world YAML, then inject Theta* waypoints (or velocity fields) into the trees and execute them with SFM inside HuNavSim/ROS2 simulators.
insight: Coupling symbolic behavior-tree structure with geometric planning improves prompt alignment, since goals come from RoI-grounded allocation rather than decoupled sampling. Presets that restrict prompts and RAG candidates cut token usage by 35-49% relative to the vanilla variant. Preliminary experiments (not tabulated) reportedly showed that removing RAG increases hallucinated nodes and latency, and that removing the global planner causes wall collisions and straight-line paths.
method: World semantic representation and RoI extraction: a human/LLM-readable world.yaml of zones, doors and entities; an LLM matches prompt tokens to RoIs and filters out irrelevant zones before building the LLM context.

BT generation with RAG: a ChromaDB store of behavior-node specs (parameters, constraints, templates) is retrieved per prompt, and an LLM (Gemini 2.5 Flash / Gemini 3 Pro, or local Qwen-3-0.6B / 4B) generates HuNavSim behavior trees as the intermediate representation.

Node wrapping: automatic ID management for agents, goals and groups is done in post-processing; queue and group behaviors are encoded as BT subtrees; a new FollowVelocityField node gives group-level flow control.

Theta* global planner on BTs: the world is decomposed into a 2D occupancy grid, and Theta* paths between consecutive GoTo goals are injected as explicit sub-goal waypoints. SFM handles local avoidance, and TRACE is an optional medium-horizon planner.

Presets: Emergency (velocity fields from Theta* paths between group centroids and a shared exit, restricted RAG), Queuing (Queue subtree with sequential goal allocation), Normal (full node set plus planner); these act as configuration overlays on the prompt, RAG set, goal sampling and planning.
RViz2 GUI and simulator integration: users enter prompts, choose presets and preview waypoints and velocity fields before running in Isaac Sim, Gazebo or Unity via ROS 2.

setting.backbone: Gemini 2.5 Flash / Gemini 3 Pro (frozen) or Qwen-3-0.6B / Qwen-3-4B (local, frozen) with RAG; Theta* and SFM for navigation
setting.observation: semantic world.yaml plus 2D occupancy grid and user text prompt
setting.action_space: behavior-tree nodes yielding waypoints / velocity fields, executed as SFM velocity commands for pedestrians
setting.simulator: Isaac Sim, Gazebo, RViz2 (ROS 2), Unity via HuNavSim 2.0
setting.privileged: hand-authored semantic world map (world.yaml) and static obstacle map

numbers_note: No navigation benchmark from the canonical list is used. The paper reports a VLM-scored (GPT-5, 0-10) scenario quality table (GROVE average: Emergency 5.33, Normal 6.57, Queuing 6.62) and a token-count table, not entered as benchmark results.
results: Under GPT-5 scoring, GROVE reaches the highest average in all presets (Emergency 5.33 vs Text-Crowd 4.43, Normal 6.57 vs TRACE 5.50, Queuing 6.62 vs Text-Crowd 4.61), with the largest gains in Prompt Alignment (e.g. Queuing 6.86 vs TRACE 2.83). Presets reduce prompt tokens by 35% / 49% / 40% (9250 / 7323 / 8575 vs about 14.3k for the vanilla variant).
limitations: High computational and inference cost from combining multiple SotA components and LLM calls.
Assumes a static obstacle map with no dynamic changes, and requires manually authored world.yaml.
Evaluation is small (N=3 scenarios per preset), qualitative/VLM-scored, and uses re-implemented baselines; no robot navigation metrics or real-robot tests.
